# Skaði: the stories first, then the spelling

Before the spelling, the story. **Skaði** earns its restoration the old way — through what was actually told.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Weregild of Þjazi.** The giant Þjazi had abducted Iðunn and her apples of youth; when Loki stole her back, Þjazi pursued in eagle shape, and the Æsir kindled a fire that scorched his wings and brought him down inside their garth, where they slew him.  Skaði took her father's death as a cause of war: she put on helmet and byrnie and came to Ásgarðr in full war-gear, and the gods chose settlement over battle. Her terms were three.

**The Feet She Chose, the Sea She Left.** Behind the screen the gods stood bare to the calves, and Skaði picked the fairest pair of feet, certain they could only belong to Baldr.  They belonged to Njǫrðr of Nóatún — the sea-god, rich and even-tempered, and entirely of the wrong element.  They agreed to divide their marriage by terrain: nine nights in Þrymheimr, then nine at Nóatún.

**The Snake above Loki.** At Ægir's feast, as Loki's flyting turns vicious, Skaði is among those he cannot charm.  She warns him that his tongue runs free only a little longer: on a sharp rock, with the guts of his own frost-cold son, the gods will bind him.  Loki answers with cruelty of his own — boasting that he was first and foremost among those who dealt Þjazi his death-blow, and claiming that Skaði once invited him to her bed.

## The Name Travels

Skaði's clearest structural parallels stand inside the Norse corpus itself: Gerðr, the giant's daughter who marries Freyr — Skaði's own stepson by Njǫrðr — so that two giant-brides enter the Vanir household a generation apart; and Ullr, named in the same chapter of Gylfaginning as an archer and snow-shoe runner, who functions almost as her male doublet, his cult the better attested of the two in Scandinavian place-names.  Etymologists have connected her name with Gothic skadus and Old English sceadu, 'shadow', and the first element of Scandinavia (Pliny's Scadinavia) has been derived from a related root — both proposals remain conjectural and debated.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Skaði** stands at [/skadi/](/skadi/) — [lore](/skadi/lore/), [scholars](/skadi/scholars/), [patterns](/skadi/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. Tier-1 is not a compliment; it is a measurement. This restoration keeps something the ASCII form provably loses, and the measurement is repeatable.
